subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: learning a rule from the mistake [Revision]
passage: The bird feeder outside the Class 5 window was Mahima's job this month. On Tuesday morning the sparrows were hopping on the empty tray, chirping at the glass. Mahima's stomach dropped. She had forgotten on Monday too. At break she went to the eco-club teacher, Suraj-sir. "Sir, I forgot to fill the feeder yesterday and today. It's my fault." "Thank you for telling me. What will you change?" Mahima thought. "I keep the seed box in the cupboard at the back, so I don't see it. And I rush in the mornings." That evening she asked her mother to set a daily reminder on her phone at 7:30, "Birds!", and the next day she moved the seed box to the window ledge right beside the feeder, where she'd see it the moment she walked in.

qa.q: Where had the seed box been kept?
qa.a: In the cupboard at the back.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel when she saw the sparrows at the empty tray?
qa.a: Guilty; her stomach dropped, since she had forgotten two days running.

qa.q: What else could Mahima do if the reminder is missed one day?
qa.a: Ask a classmate to be her back-up, so the birds are fed even on a rushed morning.

qa.q: How does Suraj-sir respond?
qa.a: He thanks her for telling him and asks what she will change, letting her find the fix herself.

grounding: After owning up to forgetting the birds, a girl sets a phone reminder with her mother and moves the seed box where she will see it.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: learning a rule from the mistake [Revision]
passage: I'm Salma, Vasudha's neighbour. Vasudha feeds the pigeons and sparrows on her balcony every morning; I can see the bowl from our kitchen. Last week, for two days, the bowl stayed empty, and the birds sat on the railing looking at her door. On the third morning I saw Vasudha talking to her mother on the balcony, pointing at the bowl. I heard her say, "I forgot. Two days. I'm sorry." Then she took her mother's phone and typed something, and her mother nodded. That afternoon Vasudha carried the seed tin out of the kitchen and put it on the balcony shelf right next to the bowl. Now the bowl is full by seven every morning. I don't know if she felt bad, but she checks it before she even brushes her teeth.

qa.q: Where did Vasudha put the seed tin?
qa.a: On the balcony shelf right next to the bowl.

qa.q: What might Vasudha have felt admitting she forgot?
qa.a: Guilty and sorry, especially with the birds waiting on the railing.

qa.q: What else could Vasudha try if she goes away for a few days?
qa.a: Ask her mother or a neighbour to fill the bowl, and show them where the tin is kept.

qa.q: How does Salma see the change?
qa.a: Salma sees the bowl full by seven every morning, though unsure whether Vasudha felt bad.

grounding: A neighbour watches a girl admit she forgot to feed the birds, set a phone reminder with her mother and keep the seed beside the bowl.

subtype: Approach: refusing and explaining why [Action]
passage:
Monday: Before maths, Deepika slid her notebook towards Preeti. "Just let me copy questions four to eight. Please. I didn't get fractions at all." Preeti's stomach tightened. "No. But I'll show you how after class. Promise." Deepika sulked and turned away.
Tuesday: Deepika didn't sit with her at lunch. Preeti felt terrible but didn't change her answer. After the last bell she waited by the gate with her notebook anyway. Deepika came, arms crossed. "Fine. Show me." They sat on the steps for twenty minutes.
Friday: In the class test, Deepika finished the fractions section and grinned across the room. At lunch she sat next to Preeti again and split her samosa without a word.

qa.q: Which questions did Deepika want to copy?
qa.a: Questions four to eight.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel on Tuesday?
qa.a: Terrible when Deepika didn't sit with her, but still firm in her answer.

qa.q: What else could Preeti have said on Monday?
qa.a: She could also have told Deepika she was worried about her, to show the no was not about the friendship.

qa.q: How does Deepika's attitude change over the week?
qa.a: From sulking to accepting help, then grinning in the test and sharing her samosa.

grounding: Over a week, a girl refuses to let a friend copy, offers to explain the method instead, and keeps the friendship.

subtype: Approach: refusing and explaining why [Action]
passage: Nitin, your friend wants to copy your homework? Let me tell you what I did when I was a girl of eleven. My best friend Rukhsana leaned over one morning and said, "Sabina, give me your arithmetic book for five minutes. Just the answers." I wanted to say yes. She was my best friend. But I also knew she would get the same sums in the exam, and my book wouldn't be sitting next to her then. So I said, "No. But come to my house after school, and I'll show you how to do them." She didn't talk to me all through recess. That evening she came anyway, with a guava in each hand. We sat on the steps till dark. And we stayed friends for sixty years.

qa.q: What did Rukhsana bring that evening?
qa.a: A guava in each hand.

qa.q: How did young Sabina feel when Rukhsana asked?
qa.a: Torn and tempted, wanting to say yes to her best friend.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story mattered most?
qa.a: Saying no but offering to teach after school, which helped Rukhsana without breaking the rule.

qa.q: How might Rukhsana have felt during recess?
qa.a: Hurt or annoyed, not talking to Sabina, before choosing to come that evening anyway.

grounding: An elder recalls refusing to let a friend copy, offering to explain the sums instead, and keeping the friendship.

subtype: Approach: thinking of what the test is for [Thinking]
passage:
"Gurpreet, pass me your answers in the test tomorrow. Just the algebra part."
"No, Pradeep."
"Why? We're friends."
"Because we're friends. Think. If you copy tomorrow, you get marks. Then what?"
"Then I pass."
"And next month is equations. Equations are built on algebra. You'll sit there and nothing will make sense, and I won't be next to you in the half-yearly."
"So you won't help me."
"I didn't say that. Copying isn't helping; it just hides the problem for one day. Come over tonight. We'll do ten sums."
"Ten?"
"Fine. Eight. With chai."
Pradeep laughed in spite of himself. "Seven o'clock?"
"Seven."

qa.q: Which part did Pradeep want to copy?
qa.a: The algebra part.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet worried about when he asked 'Then what?'
qa.a: He was worried that copying would leave Pradeep lost when equations came next month.

qa.q: What else could Gurpreet offer if one evening isn't enough?
qa.a: A few short sessions before the half-yearly, so Pradeep builds the algebra properly.

qa.q: How does Pradeep's mood change?
qa.a: From pushing for answers to laughing in spite of himself and agreeing to study.

grounding: A boy reasons aloud that copying gives marks but no learning, so helping a friend cheat would not really help him.

subtype: Approach: thinking of what the test is for [Thinking]
passage: Last year, during the science unit test, my friend Baljeet whispered, "Sachin, tilt your paper. Just a little." I remember my hand actually starting to move. Then I thought: the test is on electricity. Next month we build circuits in the lab, in pairs. If Baljeet copies my answers now, he'll get a good mark and still not know what a closed circuit is. Then in the lab he'll be lost, and I'll be doing it all. So I didn't tilt my paper. After the test he was angry. I told him, "Copying gives you marks, not the knowing. Sit with me on Saturday." He came, grumbling. In the lab next month, he was the one who got our bulb to light.

qa.q: What was the test on?
qa.a: Electricity.

qa.q: How did Sachin feel when Baljeet whispered?
qa.a: Tempted at first, with a hand starting to move, then uneasy as the thinking began.

qa.q: What else could Sachin have done after the test?
qa.a: Explained the reason to Baljeet calmly, as happened, and offered more than one study session.

qa.q: How does Baljeet seem to feel over time?
qa.a: Angry right after the test, grumbling on Saturday, and then proud when he got the bulb to light.

grounding: Looking back, a child reasons that copying gives marks but no learning, so letting a friend copy would not truly help him.

subtype: Approach: giving in to keep the friendship [Pitfall]
passage: In the maths test at their school in London, Emil nudged Kwame's elbow and mouthed, "Number six." Kwame shook his head a tiny bit. Emil's face hardened, and Kwame remembered last month, when Emil hadn't spoken to Tomasz for a whole week. So Kwame moved his arm and let his page show. Emil copied fast. Afterwards Emil grinned and slapped his back, but Kwame felt sick. That evening he kept thinking: Ms Adeyemi marks carefully. What if she noticed two identical pages? He couldn't finish his rice. The next morning he dreaded maths. By Friday, when Ms Adeyemi asked both boys to stay behind after class, the fear had grown so big he could barely look up.

qa.q: Which question did Emil want?
qa.a: Number six.

qa.q: Why did Kwame let Emil copy, and how did he feel afterwards?
qa.a: He was afraid Emil would stop talking to him; afterwards he felt sick and worried.

qa.q: What else could Kwame have done?
qa.a: Kept his arm in place and talked to Emil after the test; a friendship that ends over a refusal was not safe anyway.

qa.q: How does Emil seem to see the copying?
qa.a: As no big deal: he grins and slaps Kwame's back.

grounding: A boy shows his answers because he fears losing a friend, and his worry grows as he realises the teacher may blame both.

subtype: Approach: giving in to keep the friendship [Pitfall]
passage: In the exam hall of their school in Kochi, Harish, one row behind, hissed, "Anand, show me the map question." Anand hesitated. Harish had been his friend since Class 1, and last week Harish had stopped talking to Vivek over something tiny. So Anand slid his sheet to the edge of the desk. Harish copied. The invigilator walked past just after, glanced at both sheets and wrote something on her clipboard. Anand's heart pounded for the rest of the paper. He couldn't remember the last answer at all. At lunch Harish said, "Relax, she didn't see anything." But all week Anand jumped whenever a teacher said his name, and on Friday, when the class teacher called both of them to the staffroom, it felt as if it had been coming for days.

qa.q: What did Harish want to see?
qa.a: The map question.

qa.q: How did Anand feel after the invigilator wrote on her clipboard?
qa.a: Frightened, with his heart pounding so hard he couldn't remember the last answer.

qa.q: What else could Anand have done when Harish hissed?
qa.a: Kept his sheet where it was and offered to help Harish study after the exam instead.

qa.q: How does Harish see it?
qa.a: Casually; he tells Anand to relax because she didn't see anything.

grounding: A boy gives in to a friend's request to copy for fear of losing him, then spends the week afraid both will be blamed.

subtype: Approach: offering an honest alternative [Action]
passage:
Thursday: Mohit caught Gopika at the water tap. "The Hindi test is on Monday. Sit next to me and let me see your answers? I'll fail otherwise." Gopika shook her head. "I won't show you answers. But you're scared of failing, right? Come to my house on Sunday. We'll do the whole chapter."
Sunday: Mohit arrived at ten with his book. Gopika's mother made poha. They read the lesson aloud, took turns asking each other the questions at the back and wrote the hard spellings three times each. By one, Mohit could answer eight of the ten without looking.
Monday: Mohit finished the test early and didn't glance sideways once. Outside he said, "I think I actually passed. On my own."

qa.q: When was the Hindi test?
qa.a: On Monday.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel about Mohit's request?
qa.a: She saw he was scared of failing, and felt sympathy rather than annoyance.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Offering Sunday study, because it met Mohit's real need to pass without either of them breaking the rules.

qa.q: How did Mohit feel after the test?
qa.a: Proud and relieved that he had passed on his own. 😊

grounding: Across a few days, a girl turns down a friend's request to copy and suggests studying together, meeting his real need honestly.

subtype: Approach: offering an honest alternative [Action]
passage: Jaya, your friend wants your answers for the geography test? When I was in Class 6, my friend Farzana asked me the same thing. "Nazia, just let me look at your paper. If I fail again, Abbu will be so disappointed." I understood then that she wasn't lazy; she was frightened. So I said, "I can't show you in the test. But come to my house on Saturday, and we'll do the whole map together until you know it." She came. We drew the rivers on old newspaper until our fingers were blue. She passed that test, not with top marks, but with her own. After that, before every exam, we studied together on the Saturday. That's how I learned you can help a friend without breaking the rules.

qa.q: What did they draw on old newspaper?
qa.a: The rivers.

qa.q: How did Nazia understand Farzana's feelings?
qa.a: Nazia saw that Farzana was frightened, not lazy, and felt sympathy for her.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made the difference?
qa.a: Offering Saturday study instead of showing her paper, so Farzana could pass with her own marks.

qa.q: How might Farzana have felt passing with her own marks?
qa.a: Proud and relieved, knowing the marks were really hers.

grounding: An elder recalls offering a frightened friend a study session instead of answers, meeting her need without breaking the rules.

subtype: Approach: telling the teacher when the friend will not stop [Revision]
passage:
Monday: Akash asked Pankaj to let him copy in Wednesday's exam. Pankaj said no.
Tuesday: Akash asked again at the bus stop. Pankaj said no again. Then Akash showed him a folded chit tucked in his sock, covered in tiny formulas. "Fine. I'll manage myself." Pankaj's mouth went dry. He thought about it all evening: if Akash was caught, it would be far worse than a low mark; if he wasn't, he'd keep doing it. "Telling isn't about getting him in trouble," Pankaj decided. "It's about stopping something bigger."
Wednesday: Before the exam, Pankaj asked Mr Bhatt for a word in the corridor and told him quietly. Mr Bhatt thanked him and said he'd handle it without naming him. As the exam began, Mr Bhatt asked everyone to empty their pockets and socks onto their desks. Akash went pale, and the chit went into the bin.

qa.q: Where had Akash hidden the chit?
qa.a: In his sock.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel when he saw the chit?
qa.a: Nervous and worried; his mouth went dry.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Telling Mr Bhatt privately before the exam, because it stopped the cheating without a public scene or naming Akash.

qa.q: What was the exam like for Akash?
qa.a: He went pale and had to throw the chit away, stopped before he could be caught using it.

grounding: After refusing twice, a boy learns his friend plans to bring a chit into the exam and quietly tells the teacher to stop a bigger problem.

subtype: Approach: telling the teacher when the friend will not stop [Revision]
passage: Suraj, you're asking whether telling a teacher makes you a tell-tale? Let me tell you something from my school days. My friend Mukul asked to copy from me before the final exam. I said no. He asked again. No. Then, the day before, he showed me the formulas he'd written on the inside of his wrist, under his watch strap. I, Varun, lay awake that night. If he was caught in the finals, it could cost him the whole year. I decided that keeping quiet was not being a good friend. So in the morning I spoke quietly to our class teacher. She thanked me, and before the paper she asked everyone to put their watches on the front desk. Mukul was angry with me for a month. Then he wasn't. Years later, he thanked me.

qa.q: Where had Mukul written the formulas?
qa.a: On the inside of his wrist, under his watch strap.

qa.q: How did young Varun feel that night?
qa.a: Worried and torn, lying awake over what to do.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made the difference?
qa.a: Speaking quietly to the teacher before the paper, which stopped a much bigger problem for Mukul.

qa.q: How did Mukul feel about it over time?
qa.a: Angry for a month, then not, and years later grateful.

grounding: An elder recalls refusing a friend twice, then telling the teacher about his hidden formulas to prevent a bigger problem.

subtype: Approach: thinking that everyone does it [Pitfall]
passage: Omkar, everyone copies, you say? I said the same. When I was in Class 7, half our class used to peep at each other's papers. I told myself it was normal, just how tests worked. So in the half-yearly science paper, I, Neelam, leaned over to look at my neighbour's diagram of the heart. The next moment the teacher's hand was on my paper. She took it away and wrote "Copying" across the top in red. I said, "But everyone does it!" She said, "Then everyone is breaking the rule. You are the one I saw." I got zero in that paper, and my mother had to come to school. I cried all the way home. Everyone did it, but I was the one who paid.

qa.q: What did the teacher write across the top of the paper?
qa.a: "Copying", in red.

qa.q: How did young Neelam feel on the way home?
qa.a: Upset and ashamed, crying all the way.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story would you change?
qa.a: Leaning over to look; answering the diagram on her own, even if others were copying, would have avoided the zero.

qa.q: How might Neelam's mother have felt being called to school?
qa.a: Disappointed and worried about what had happened.

grounding: An elder recalls believing copying was normal because half the class did it, then being caught and facing the consequences.

subtype: Approach: thinking that everyone does it [Pitfall]
passage: The maths test had started late because of a power cut, and now there were only twenty minutes left for thirty sums. The fan was off, the room was hot, and Reena was stuck on question twelve. Around her she could see heads tilting, eyes sliding sideways. "Half the class does it," she told herself. "It's normal." She glanced at Dilnaz's page and started copying the working. A shadow fell across her desk. The teacher picked up Reena's paper. "Reena. Come to the front." "Ma'am, everyone was looking!" "Then I'll watch everyone more closely. But I saw you." Reena got zero for the test and a note home. That evening she stared at the note for a long time, and the word "everyone" felt very small.

qa.q: How many sums were left for the last twenty minutes?
qa.a: Thirty sums.

qa.q: What did Reena tell herself, and how did she feel that evening?
qa.a: That half the class copies so it's normal; by evening she felt ashamed, and the excuse felt very small.

qa.q: What else could Reena have done when she got stuck on question twelve?
qa.a: Skipped it and moved on to sums she could do, coming back if time was left.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel about what happened?
qa.a: Dilnaz may feel uncomfortable that her page was copied, and worried about being involved.

grounding: Under time pressure, a girl tells herself copying is normal because others do it, then is caught and faces the consequences.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing a light reply to avoid a fight [Thinking]
passage: On the auto ride to school in Pune, Pradeep went over it in his head. Yesterday Sarita had hinted she'd ask to copy his English homework today, like last week. Last week he'd said, "That's cheating," and she'd sulked for two days. "That made it about her," he thought. "As if I was calling her a cheat." What if he made it about himself instead? He practised under his breath: "Sorry, I can't. Ma'am compared my book with Rohan's last time, and I really don't want any trouble." It was true, and it didn't point at her at all. At the gate Sarita came up. "Pradeep, English?" He said his line. She shrugged. "Okay, fair." And she walked with him to class, chatting about cricket.

qa.q: How long did Sarita sulk last week?
qa.a: Two days.

qa.q: What was Pradeep thinking as he rehearsed?
qa.a: He was worried about hurting Sarita again and wanted a refusal that didn't sound like judging her.

qa.q: What else could Pradeep offer Sarita?
qa.a: To go over the English homework with her at lunch, so she isn't left stuck.

qa.q: How does Sarita react this time?
qa.a: Sarita shrugs, says 'Okay, fair', and walks with him chatting about cricket.

grounding: A boy prepares a refusal about his own wish to avoid trouble rather than judging his friend, which makes it easier to accept.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing a light reply to avoid a fight [Thinking]
passage:
"Lalit, pass me your science worksheet. Five minutes."
"Can't, Zubin. Sir caught two people last week with the same answers, and he said next time he's calling parents. I really don't want my Papa in the staffroom."
"He won't notice."
"He noticed Kiran's. And Kiran changed the words."
"Hmm. True. That was scary."
"I've already got enough trouble with my handwriting marks. I can't add this."
"Okay, okay. But I don't get question three."
"Question three I can explain. That's not copying. Come here."
"You're not angry with me for asking?"
"Why would I be? I just don't want to end up in the staffroom."
Zubin grinned and pulled his chair closer.

qa.q: What did Sir say he'd do next time?
qa.a: Call parents.

qa.q: How does Lalit feel while refusing?
qa.a: Calm but a bit worried about trouble, and not angry with Zubin at all.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Giving a reason about himself, so Zubin didn't feel judged, and then offering to explain question three.

qa.q: How does Zubin take the refusal?
qa.a: Zubin accepts it and grins, relieved that Lalit isn't angry with him.

grounding: A boy refuses to share answers with a reason about avoiding trouble himself, not judging his friend, which keeps things friendly.

subtype: Approach: tempted by fear of failing [Thinking]
passage:
Class teacher's note, Wednesday.
After today's maths test, Sumit stayed back. He told me something honest: during the test his eyes kept going to his neighbour's page. "I didn't copy, Ma'am. But I wanted to. I got scared I'd fail again, and then I wanted to look." He had worked it out himself: "It's not that I'm a cheater. It's that I'm scared. If I wasn't scared, I wouldn't want to look." Then he asked if I could give him extra practice in division, because that is where he feels lost. I told him I was glad he had told me. We have agreed on fifteen minutes after class on Tuesdays and Thursdays. I will also let his parents know that he asked for help himself.
Minakshi, class teacher

qa.q: When will the extra practice happen?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes after class on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

qa.q: What did Sumit realise about why he wanted to look?
qa.a: That fear of failing made cheating tempting; he felt scared, not dishonest.

qa.q: What else could help Sumit before the next test?
qa.a: Practising a few division sums at home each day, so he walks in less afraid.

qa.q: How does Minakshi respond?
qa.a: Minakshi is glad he told her, sets up extra help, and plans to tell his parents he asked himself.

grounding: A teacher's note records a boy noticing that fear of low marks made peeking tempting, and asking for extra help instead.

subtype: Approach: tempted by fear of failing [Thinking]
passage:
Friday
Today in the English test I almost looked at Ayesha's paper. She sits so close, and I was stuck on the grammar part, and I kept thinking, what if I get a four again, what if Papa's face does that disappointed thing. My eyes started moving on their own. Then I stopped and thought: why do I want to look? Not because I'm bad. Because I'm scared. The scared feeling is doing the pulling. So I left that answer blank. After class I went to Mrs Rao and asked if she could help me with grammar before the next test. She said yes, Monday lunch. I feel lighter than I thought I would.
Varun

qa.q: When will Mrs Rao help?
qa.a: At Monday lunch.

qa.q: What did Varun realise about the pull to look?
qa.a: That the scared feeling about a low mark was doing the pulling, not being a bad person.

qa.q: What else could Varun do before Monday?
qa.a: Varun could note which grammar questions were hardest, so the time with Mrs Rao goes further.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rao see Varun's request?
qa.a: Mrs Rao seems glad to help, agreeing straight away to Monday lunch.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child noticing that fear of low marks makes cheating tempting and asking the teacher for extra help.

subtype: Approach: asking a parent what to do about a friend [Action]
passage: In their village near Ludhiana, Amandeep helped her mother roll rotis while working up her courage. "Mummy, Devika copies from my notebook every day before the teacher comes. She says if I tell, she won't be my friend." Her mother kept rolling. "What do you think you should do?" "I don't know. Telling feels mean. Not telling feels like lying." Her mother put down the rolling pin. "Can you be kind and honest both? First talk to Devika yourself. Tell her you won't give the notebook any more, and offer to do homework together after school. If she keeps copying from others, then tell the teacher, and say you're worried for her, not angry." Amandeep flipped a roti, thinking. "Tomorrow. At the handpump."

qa.q: When does Devika copy?
qa.a: Every day before the teacher comes.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel about telling?
qa.a: Torn: telling felt mean, but not telling felt like lying.

qa.q: What else could Amandeep do if Devika gets angry?
qa.a: Keep offering homework together, and still go to the teacher if the copying continues, as Mummy suggested.

qa.q: How might Devika feel when Amandeep talks to her?
qa.a: Maybe hurt or defensive at first, but she may see that Amandeep cares and is offering help.

grounding: A girl unsure about telling on a friend talks it over with her mother, who helps her find a way to be kind and honest together.

subtype: Approach: asking a parent what to do about a friend [Action]
passage: After swimming practice in Lagos, Amara sat in the car beside her mum, picking at her towel. "Mum, if a friend is cheating, is it wrong to tell?" Her mum turned down the radio. "Tell me what happened." "Olga has the answers to the spelling tests. Her older brother had the same teacher. She shares them with some girls. She offered them to me." "What did you say?" "No. But now I don't know if I should tell Mrs Okafor. Olga's my friend." Her mum thought for a moment. "You can be kind and truthful together. Talk to Olga first; tell her you're worried she'll get into real trouble. If it carries on, tell Mrs Okafor privately, and say you're worried, not angry. That's being a friend too." Amara nodded slowly and pulled the towel tighter.

qa.q: Where did Olga get the answers?
qa.a: From her older brother, who had the same teacher.

qa.q: How was Amara feeling in the car?
qa.a: Torn and uneasy, picking at her towel.

qa.q: What else could Amara do before talking to Olga?
qa.a: Think of how to say it gently, perhaps offering to practise spellings together.

qa.q: How might Olga feel when Amara talks to her?
qa.a: Olga may feel embarrassed or defensive, but may also see that Amara is worried for her.

grounding: A girl unsure whether to report a friend's cheating talks with her mother, who helps her be both kind and honest.
